name: deferred-validation
intent: Postpone validating an object until an action actually needs its contents, so that work in progress can exist incomplete and every check is sized to the use that triggers it.
problem: Validation is placed at ingestion - constructor, setter, deserialiser - so that an invalid object cannot exist; but real systems must carry drafts, historical records and partially filled forms, and different actions need different guarantees: saving a draft needs presence checks, publishing needs cross-field and cross-aggregate consistency, and reading legacy data must not fail because a field nobody uses is absent. Eager validation either rejects legitimate data or makes every use site pay for the strictest check.
context: Domain models and boundary payloads that are assembled over time (multi-step forms, imports, ORM materialisation, PATCH requests), where one object is used by several actions with different trust levels and where the cost or reach of a check depends on the action requested. Applies whenever an object can be valid for one use and invalid for another.
benefits: Incomplete work becomes representable: a draft, an imported record or a partially bound payload travels through the program without sentinel values or exception-driven control flow.

Checks are sized to the action: a save runs the cheap subset, publication runs presence, type, cross-field and cross-aggregate checks in ordered passes, so expensive rules are not paid on paths that never need them.
Validation rules move out of setters into use-named operations and rule objects, which removes the context-free invariant enforcement that makes entities unloadable from legacy data.
Errors can be reported in the shape the consumer needs: one deferred pass fills a violation set, a Result or field-level messages, instead of throwing on the first problem from inside a setter.
Failure surfaces where it can still be handled - at the action boundary, with the operation and the principal in scope - rather than deep inside a constructor or a deserialisation callback.
tradeoffs: Invalid state exists inside the program between ingestion and use: every consumer must pass the gate, and a forgotten call silently defeats the pattern with no compile-time help.

Feedback is late by construction: the user learns about a defect when the action runs, so the pattern usually needs companion machinery (echo back, visible implications, previews) to keep the loop short.
A validator placed outside the object must see otherwise-hidden state, so encapsulation is weakened; keeping the check in a use-named operation on the object is the usual repair.
The per-action check sets drift: the save-time and publish-time rules live in different places and quietly disagree until the day the missing check matters.

Verdicts must be either recomputed (cost) or memoised (staleness): a cached valid result survives a later mutation unless it is invalidated by a mutation epoch, and re-checking on every access can dominate the use itself.
Late is not free: the gate must run before the first irreversible effect, or the deferral only postpones the damage to a published message, an external call or a committed transaction.

In large object graphs (e.g., ORM materialisation), cascading deferred validation can trigger N+1-style traversal and expensive cycle detection on each gate invocation, especially with Bean Validation's cascading validation across related entities.

The pattern trades compile-time safety for runtime flexibility: unlike type-level 'parse, don't validate' approaches that make illegal states unrepresentable, deferred validation defers correctness to runtime checks that can still be bypassed.

participants.responsibility: Holds possibly incomplete state and exposes use-named validation operations; it does not enforce invariants at assignment or construction time.
The requested operation (save, compute, publish) that decides when validation runs and how much is required; it is the trigger, not the data.
Encodes the anticipated use (validateForSave, validateForPublication) and delegates to simpler operations in ordered passes, so a stricter use includes all weaker checks.
One validation rule and its composition (rule objects, constraint annotations, validator functions) that reads the candidate and reports violations.
Accumulates violations so one pass reports every problem, most specific first, and lets the caller decide how to present them.
The action boundary that invokes the gate before the irreversible step: persist, publish, send, or hand data to another trust zone.

use_cases: Multi-step forms and wizards: each step saves a draft with presence checks only, and the submit action runs the full rule set.
Loading legacy or migrated data into a domain model: entities materialise with missing or unknown fields and are validated when an operation actually acts on them.
ORM and serializer materialisation: an object is built field by field without running setters, and the deferred gate runs before flush or commit.
PATCH and partial-update APIs: the payload is checked against the fields the operation will consume, not against the entity's full invariant set.
Import and batch pipelines: records are parsed cheaply and only the rows selected for publication are checked, with violations collected into a report instead of aborting the batch.
Anti-corruption layers: unknown or not-yet-mapped fields are carried through translation and rejected only when the domain operation that needs them runs.

CQRS command validation: commands arriving at an aggregate are validated only when the aggregate processes them, supporting command-level draft states and post-dispatch validation in the domain layer rather than at the boundary.

Event sourcing reconstruction: aggregates are rehydrated from an event stream where early events may reflect schema that no longer applies; validation is deferred until the aggregate receives its next command.

Type-first parse-don't-validate gateway: raw input is parsed into an intermediate representation (possibly with unknown/missing fields) that carries through the system; the type-level guarantee is established at construction rather than by validating at the boundary.

Bean Validation (JSR-303/JSR-380) group sequencing: validation groups define ordered passes (e.g., Default → Extended → Premium) where each group represents a use case's required checks, and group conversion sequences the gates without re-running cheap checks.

Django ORM and Django REST Framework: model.save() deliberately does not call full_clean() - clean_fields, clean, validate_unique and validate_constraints are an explicit gate the caller invokes, with every error collected into message_dict - and DRF requires serializer.is_valid() before save(), accumulating field-level errors in serializer.errors or converting them to HTTP 400 via raise_exception=True.

Rails Active Record: validations run at save time rather than at assignment, are scoped per use by validation context (on: :create / :update or custom contexts like :account_setup via valid?(context)), and save(validate: false) is the documented per-action bypass.

Hibernate ORM Bean Validation integration: entities are validated on the pre-insert and pre-update lifecycle events just before flush, and the check set per event is selected by group (javax.persistence.validation.group.pre-persist/-update/-remove), so the persistence action itself names the gate and its rule subset.
avoid_when: The value must always be valid and is cheap to check (identifiers, money, quantities): construct it validated and let the type carry the guarantee.
Exactly one action consumes the object and the rule is a simple precondition: a guard clause at that single entry point is smaller and just as safe.

The data is untrusted and crosses a security boundary: validate at the boundary (intercepting validator, reference monitor), because deferral widens the window in which hostile bytes travel through the program.
A late failure is unacceptable (hard real-time, safety-relevant, irreversible external effects) and the check is affordable up front: validate eagerly and fail fast.

The system uses type-first design where algebraic data types can make illegal states unrepresentable: in languages with rich sum-type support (Rust, Haskell, F#, TypeScript discriminated unions), parsing raw input into domain types at the boundary eliminates the need for deferred runtime checks.

Validation groups would need to proliferate beyond manageability: when every action requires a distinct group and composition rules become complex, a simpler single-pass validation or specification-based approach scales better.
anti_patterns: Validation by convention only: every gate is optional and at least one action skips it, so invalid records reach publication or storage - deferred validation without a mandatory gate is missing validation.
Eager entity: setters throw on invalid assignment, so historical loads, imports and drafts fail, and the wording of error messages ends up owned by the entity.
One global validator that reaches into every object's fields, duplicating rules and turning the domain model into a property bag that exists only to be inspected.
Cached verdict without an epoch: a memoised is-valid flag survives later mutation and reports stale validity to the next action.
Deferring past the side effect: the record is validated after the message was published or the transaction committed, which is when the check stops being useful.
Validation inside setters as a substitute for domain logic: setters that throw on every invalid assignment make entities unloadable from legacy data and push business rules into data-access code.

Type proliferation from parse-don't-validate taken too far: creating a new type per validation context (DraftOrder, SubmittedOrder, PaidOrder) without clear lifecycle boundaries creates an unmanageable type graph.

Duplicate validation across layers: boundary validation (DTO/command), application-layer validation, and domain-layer validation each re-implement the same rules, so changes to business rules require updates in N places.
design_principles: Separate what is valid from when it is checked: validity is a property of the data, timing is a policy of the use.
Fail at the last responsible moment: no irreversible effect before the gate for that action.
Single responsibility for rules: rules live in rule objects or validators, not in setters and not in the callers.
Complete mediation on the exit path: whatever leaves the component passes the check for that exit.
Explicit over implicit: name validation operations after the use they validate, so the required checks can be read from the call graph.

Parse once, validate at boundaries; trust types through the core: raw external data is parsed into domain types at system entry, after which internal code relies on type guarantees rather than re-validating.
Layer validation by concern: input/shape validation at the boundary, domain invariants in the aggregate, cross-aggregate rules in sagas or domain services - not all in one place.
best_practices: Name validation operations after the use (validateForSave, validateForPublication) and have them delegate to simpler ones, so stricter actions include the weaker checks instead of re-implementing them.
Run the gate before the irreversible step - flush, publish, send, external call - never after.
Collect violations instead of throwing on the first: check in passes, with required quantities present before their consistency, and report the most specific problems first.
Cache a verdict only with a mutation epoch or version, otherwise recompute the cheap checks on each use.
Make the gate unavoidable at the action boundary: one entry point per action calls the matching validation operation, so the pattern does not depend on every caller remembering.
Keep incompleteness explicit - absent values as Option/Optional/Null variants or a labelled exceptional value - rather than sentinel strings that a later check cannot distinguish from real data.
Report through the layer that owns the wording: the domain returns violations or a Result, message text belongs to the presentation or API layer.

Use validation groups (Bean Validation JSR-380 Default, GroupSequence) to sequence passes without re-running cheap checks: order groups so cheaper checks run first and fail-fast mode exits on the first violation in high-stakes paths.
Combine with the Notification pattern: accumulate all violations in a collector so callers receive complete feedback rather than a single first error.
For large object graphs, configure fail-fast mode or restrict cascading validation (@Valid) to only the fields the action actually consumes to avoid expensive cycle detection on each gate.

In CQRS/event-sourced systems, validate commands at two layers: basic input shape at the boundary, full invariants inside the aggregate on command dispatch - this separates cheap shape checks from expensive domain logic.

Consider parse-don't-validate for high-value fields: at the boundary, parse raw input into domain types (e.g., NonEmptyString, PositiveInt) that make illegal values unrepresentable, then trust those types through the core and reserve deferred validation for context-dependent rules only.
Document the per-action rule sets in a central registry or validation matrix so drift between save-time and publish-time rules is visible and auditable.
sources: Ward Cunningham, The CHECKS Pattern Language of Information Integrity (PLoP '94; in Pattern Languages of Program Design), pattern 6 'Deferred Validation' - delay detailed validation of a domain model until an action is requested and tailor the extent of the validation to that action.

Vaughn Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013) - validation discussed with deferred validation as an alternative to always-valid entities (as cited by the Microsoft architecture guide below).
Microsoft, .NET Microservices Architecture for Containerized .NET Applications - 'Designing validations in the domain model layer', section 'Use deferred validation in the domain'.
Jeffrey Palermo, The fallacy of the always-valid entity (2009) - validation belongs outside the entity and runs when the operation does.
Kamil Grzybek, Domain Model Validation (2019) - compares the validation-object, deferred-validation and always-valid strategies and names the encapsulation cost of deferred validation.
Martin Fowler, Notification Pattern (2004) - accumulates multiple validation errors during an operation to avoid stopping at the first failure, aligned with deferred validation's violation collector.
Martin Fowler, Replacing Throwing Exceptions with Notification in Validations (2011) - refactoring from fail-fast exceptions to a Notification collector that enables callers to inspect all errors.

Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2004) - aggregate invariant enforcement and the role of specification pattern in expressing validation rules; deferred validation relates to specification as the expression of contextual validation criteria.

Martin Fowler with ribs, Specification Pattern Paper (1998) - separates 'how to match' from the candidate, enabling use in selection, validation, and build-to-order; composite specification enables deferred validation's composable rule sets.

Alexis King (lexi-lambda), Parse, Don't Validate (2019) - contrasts parsing (which returns a refined type preserving knowledge) with validation (which discards it); argues for making illegal states unrepresentable through type construction rather than runtime checks.

Yaron Minsky / Functional Software Architecture, Make Illegal States Unrepresentable - design data models so illegal states cannot be represented by the type system; uses parse-don't-validate to centralize validation at boundaries.

Steve Smith, Parse, Don't Validate – DevIQ (2023) - practical application of parse-don't-validate: parse at boundaries into domain types, then trust types through the core eliminating repeated re-validation.
Vladimir Khorikov, Specification pattern in the DDD trilemma (2021) - specification pattern as a way to encode domain validation that trades domain model purity for encapsulation and reusability.

Jay Freestone, You might not need the always-valid entity (2024) - critiques always-valid entity in DDD; argues validity is contextual and core invariants should be guarded inside the entity while broader contextual rules belong in specifications.
Vladimir Khorikov, Validation and DDD (2017) - four validation approaches for DDD aggregates: self-validating entity, validation object, deferred validation, and invariant shields.
Jimmy Bogard, Validation in a DDD world (2009) - true validation is context-driven and operation-centric, not an IsValid check on entities; validation depends on the operation being performed.

Enterprise Craftsmanship, When to validate commands in CQRS? (2022) - validates commands after dispatch in command handlers and domain layer rather than at the boundary, aligning with deferred validation's domain-layer gate.

Hibernate Validator 9.x Reference Guide (2025) - Jakarta Bean Validation (JSR-380) validation groups, group sequencing, fail-fast mode, and performance considerations for cascading validation in large object graphs.

In Relation To Blog, Faster Than Ever: A Look at Hibernate Validator 9.1's Performance (2025) - performance improvements in cascading validation through stack-based bean tracking, reducing memory allocations and cycle detection overhead.

Django documentation, Model instance reference - full_clean() runs clean_fields(), clean(), validate_unique() and validate_constraints() in order and collects every error into ValidationError.message_dict, but model.save() deliberately does not call it: model-level validation is an explicit gate the caller must invoke.

Django REST Framework, Serializer API guide - is_valid() must be called before save() or access to validated_data; errors accumulate in serializer.errors and raise_exception=True turns them into an HTTP 400 at the API boundary.

Ruby on Rails Guides, Active Record Validations - validations run on save rather than on assignment, are scoped by validation context (on: :create/:update, custom contexts, valid?(context)), and save(validate: false) skips the gate.

Hibernate ORM documentation, Additional modules / Bean Validation integration - the BeanValidationEventListener validates entities on pre-insert and pre-update before changes reach the database, with per-event validation groups configurable via javax.persistence.validation.group.pre-persist/-update/-remove and violations surfacing as ConstraintViolationException (RollbackException at commit).

Piotr Solnica (dry-rb creator), Invalid Object Is An Anti-Pattern (criticism, 2023) - the opposing view: objects carried in invalid states crash consumers and defeat type safety; boundary-parsed constrained types should shrink the window in which partial data travels, confining deferred validation to genuinely contextual rules.
